title: "The Triangle of Everything"
engine: markdown
pyodide:
  packages:
    - numpy
    - pandas

---

In 2023, two astrophysicists published a chart that placed **every
object in the Universe on one pair of axes**: quarks, viruses, fleas,
whales, planets, stars, black holes, galaxies, and the observable Universe
itself (Lineweaver & Patel, *All objects and some questions*, American
Journal of Physics 91:819). In this part you will rebuild that chart, step by step.



```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import js
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import altair as alt
from pyodide.http import open_url

# Data files live beside this page; the Python worker runs from site_libs/.
DATA_URL = js.location.href.split("site_libs/")[0] + "data/"

alt.data_transformers.enable("default", max_rows=12_000)

# Physical constants, cgs units (grams, centimetres, seconds)
G    = 6.674e-8       # gravitational constant [cm^3 g^-1 s^-2]
c    = 2.998e10       # speed of light [cm/s]
hbar = 1.055e-27      # reduced Planck constant [erg s]
H0   = 70 / 3.086e19  # Hubble constant: 70 km/s/Mpc, converted to [1/s]

print("Environment ready.")
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| include: false
# Pre-build every name the page uses, so each cell works no matter which
# cells were run before it. The visible cells re-derive all of this.
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
objects = pd.read_csv(open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv"))
rows = objects.astype(str).values.tolist()
names  = objects["name"].tolist()
groups = objects["group"].tolist()
mass   = objects["mass_g"].to_numpy()
radius = objects["radius_cm"].to_numpy()

group_colours = {
    "particles":         "#666666",
    "life":              "#30a8b1",
    "worlds":            "#4269d0",
    "stars":             "#c98a00",
    "black holes":       "#171717",
    "cosmic structures": "#9475cd",
}

LABEL_LEFT  = {"Higgs boson", "white dwarf", "globular cluster"}
LABEL_BELOW = {"neutron star", "Ceres"}

GROUP_DOMAIN = list(group_colours)
GROUP_RANGE = [group_colours[group] for group in GROUP_DOMAIN]

def cosmos_x(field="radius_cm"):
    return alt.X(
        f"{field}:Q",
        title="radius (cm)",
        scale=alt.Scale(type="log", domain=[1e-35, 1e30], nice=False),
        axis=alt.Axis(grid=True, tickCount=14, format=".0e"),
    )

def cosmos_y(field="mass_g"):
    return alt.Y(
        f"{field}:Q",
        title="mass (g)",
        scale=alt.Scale(type="log", domain=[1e-40, 1e60], nice=False),
        axis=alt.Axis(grid=True, tickCount=11, format=".0e"),
    )

def group_colour(show_legend=True):
    legend = alt.Legend(title="Object group") if show_legend else None
    return alt.Color(
        "group:N",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=GROUP_DOMAIN, range=GROUP_RANGE),
        legend=legend,
    )

def object_layers(table=objects, show_legend=True, point_size=55):
    points = alt.Chart(table).mark_circle(size=point_size).encode(
        x=cosmos_x(),
        y=cosmos_y(),
        color=group_colour(show_legend),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("name:N", title="Object"),
            alt.Tooltip("group:N", title="Group"),
            alt.Tooltip("mass_g:Q", title="Mass (g)", format=".2e"),
            alt.Tooltip("radius_cm:Q", title="Radius (cm)", format=".2e"),
        ],
    )

    left = table[table["name"].isin(LABEL_LEFT)]
    below = table[table["name"].isin(LABEL_BELOW)]
    regular = table[~table["name"].isin(LABEL_LEFT | LABEL_BELOW)]

    def labels(data, **mark_options):
        return alt.Chart(data).mark_text(fontSize=10, **mark_options).encode(
            x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="name:N",
            color=group_colour(False),
        )

    return (
        points
        + labels(regular, align="left", dx=6)
        + labels(left, align="right", dx=-6)
        + labels(below, align="left", dx=6, dy=10)
    )

r_line = np.logspace(-35, 30, 200)

def mass_at_density(rho, r):
    return 4/3 * np.pi * rho * r**3

def schwarzschild_mass(r):
    return r * c**2 / (2 * G)

def compton_mass(r):
    return hbar / (r * c)

rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)
l_p = np.sqrt(hbar * G / c**3)
m_p = np.sqrt(hbar * c / G)
r_x = np.sqrt(2 * G * hbar / c**3)
m_x = np.sqrt(hbar * c / (2 * G))
rho_human = rho_all[names.index("human")]
iU = names.index("observable Universe")
ratio = 2 * G * mass[iU] / c**2 / radius[iU]

density_lines = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({
        "radius_cm": r_line,
        "mass_g": mass_at_density(rho, r_line),
        "density": label,
    })
    for rho, label in [(1.0, "atomic density"),
                       (2.3e14, "nuclear density")]
], ignore_index=True)
density_line_chart = alt.Chart(density_lines).mark_line(
    color="#888888", strokeDash=[7, 5], strokeWidth=1.2, clip=True
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), detail="density:N")

density_label_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [2e14, 2e2],
    "mass_g": [mass_at_density(1, 1e14),
               mass_at_density(2.3e14, 1e2)],
    "label": ["atomic density", "nuclear density"],
})
density_labels = alt.Chart(density_label_data).mark_text(
    angle=297, align="left", dx=5, color="#777777", fontSize=11
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

wall_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": r_line,
    "gravity_mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
    "compton_mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
    "upper_mass_g": 1e60,
    "lower_mass_g": 1e-40,
})
gravity_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#e66852", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y("gravity_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("upper_mass_g:Q"),
)
quantum_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#4269d0", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y("lower_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("compton_mass_g:Q"),
)
wall_lines = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "black-hole limit"}),
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "Compton limit"}),
], ignore_index=True)
wall_line_chart = alt.Chart(wall_lines).mark_line(
    color="#171717", strokeWidth=1.5, clip=True
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), detail="wall:N")
```

## 1 · One pair of axes for everything

What would a graph of everything compare?
Mass and radius are the two properties **every physical
object has**. But from a neutrino to the observable Universe, mass spans
about **90 orders of magnitude** and radius about **44**. This means both axes must be
logarithmic.

::: {.callout-tip title="Powers of Ten"}
Watch the nine-minute 1977 short film [*Powers of Ten*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0fKBhvDjuy0) before
continuing. Notice how changing scale changes which objects and relationships
can be seen.
:::

The chart's raw material is a curated table with one row per object; name,
group, mass and radius:

```{pyodide}
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
objects = pd.read_csv(open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv"))
rows = objects.astype(str).values.tolist()
names  = objects["name"].tolist()
groups = objects["group"].tolist()
mass   = objects["mass_g"].to_numpy()
radius = objects["radius_cm"].to_numpy()

print(f"{'name':<22} {'group':<18} {'mass':>13} {'radius':>14}")
print("-" * 70)
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r[0]:<22} {r[1]:<18} {float(r[2]):>10.2e} g {float(r[3]):>10.2e} cm")
print(f"\n{len(names)} objects in total")
```

```{pyodide}
assert len(names) == 29
assert mass.max() / mass.min() > 1e89
assert radius.max() / radius.min() > 1e43
print("✓ 29 objects; mass spans 90 orders of magnitude, radius spans 44")
```

Start with five more familiar objects:

```{pyodide}
FAMILIAR = ["flea", "human", "blue whale", "Earth", "Sun"]

familiar = objects[objects["name"].isin(FAMILIAR)]

familiar_base = alt.Chart(familiar).encode(
    x=alt.X("radius_cm:Q", title="radius (cm)",
            scale=alt.Scale(type="log", nice=False)),
    y=alt.Y("mass_g:Q", title="mass (g)",
            scale=alt.Scale(type="log", nice=False)),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("name:N", title="Object"),
        alt.Tooltip("mass_g:Q", title="Mass (g)", format=".2e"),
        alt.Tooltip("radius_cm:Q", title="Radius (cm)", format=".2e"),
    ],
)

familiar_points = familiar_base.mark_circle(size=80, color="#4269d0")
familiar_labels = familiar_base.mark_text(
    align="left", dx=7, fontSize=12, color="#4269d0"
).encode(text="name:N")

(familiar_points + familiar_labels).properties(
    width=720,
    height=420,
    title="Five familiar objects: 37 orders of magnitude in mass",
).configure_axis(gridColor="#dddddd", gridOpacity=0.7)
```

Notice that they fall roughly on a straight line.

Before interpreting that line, ask what **radius** means for a human. A human
is not a sphere. The table assigns the human a mass of 70 kg and a radius of
50 cm, where 50 cm is a convenient measure of characteristic size. What would
happen if we mistakenly treated it as a literal spherical radius?

```{pyodide}
i = names.index("human")
sphere_volume_cm3 = 4/3 * np.pi * radius[i]**3
sphere_volume_litres = sphere_volume_cm3 / 1000
rho_human = mass[i] / sphere_volume_cm3

print(f"volume of a sphere with radius 50 cm: {sphere_volume_litres:.0f} litres")
print(f"70 kg divided by that volume: {rho_human:.2f} g/cm³")
```

::: {.callout-important title="Approximate Magnitude"}
A 70 kg human has a volume of roughly 70 litres because the human body is
close to the density of water. The calculation gives 524 litres only because
we forced the 50 cm characteristic size into a formula for a sphere. The
result does **not** show that humans have a density of 0.13 g/cm³.

This is a warning about the axis. Radius is a geometric measurement for a
planet or star, but an approximate characteristic size for an irregular object
such as a flea, human or whale. The chart is designed for comparisons across
many orders of magnitude, not precise estimates of each object's density.
:::

The interesting thing is where the points
**aren't**:  Nothing in the top-left (small but extremely heavy), nothing
in the bottom-right (huge but almost massless). Two whole corners of
possibility, empty. Why?

## 3 · Lines of constant density

Any object of roughly uniform density $\rho$ obeys
$m = \frac{4}{3}\pi \rho\, r^3$. Take logs and this becomes
$\log m = 3\log r + \text{const}$: on our axes, **a straight line of
slope 3**, one line per density. Chemistry pins atomic matter near
$\rho \approx 1\ \text{g/cm}^3$; nuclear matter sits fourteen decades
higher:

```{pyodide}
r_line = np.logspace(-35, 30, 200)

def mass_at_density(rho, r):
    return 4/3 * np.pi * rho * r**3

density_lines = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({
        "radius_cm": r_line,
        "mass_g": mass_at_density(rho, r_line),
        "density": label,
    })
    for rho, label in [(1.0, "atomic density"),
                       (2.3e14, "nuclear density")]
], ignore_index=True)

density_line_chart = alt.Chart(density_lines).mark_line(
    color="#888888", strokeDash=[7, 5], strokeWidth=1.2, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(),
    y=cosmos_y(),
    detail="density:N",
)

density_label_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [2e14, 2e2],
    "mass_g": [mass_at_density(1, 1e14),
               mass_at_density(2.3e14, 1e2)],
    "label": ["atomic density", "nuclear density"],
})

density_labels = alt.Chart(density_label_data).mark_text(
    angle=297, align="left", dx=5, color="#777777", fontSize=11
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N"
)

(density_line_chart + object_layers() + density_labels).properties(
    width=740,
    height=650,
    title="Two densities organise almost everything",
).configure_axis(gridColor="#dddddd", gridOpacity=0.7)
```

Suddenly the scatter has a skeleton. Everything made of atoms (viruses,
fleas, whales, asteroids, planets, the Sun) strings out along the atomic
line: that *was* the straight line hiding in the five familiar objects.
The proton and the neutron star, nineteen decades apart in size, share the
nuclear line: **a neutron star really is matter at the density of an
atomic nucleus, the size of a city**.

```{pyodide}
rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)

i_ns, i_p = names.index("neutron star"), names.index("proton")
assert 1e14 < rho_all[i_ns] < 1e15 and 1e14 < rho_all[i_p] < 1e15
assert rho_all[names.index("red giant")] < 1e-5
print("✓ proton and neutron star both sit at nuclear density, ~10¹⁴ g/cm³")
print(f"densest object:  {names[int(np.argmax(rho_all))]}")
print(f"fluffiest object: {names[int(np.argmin(rho_all))]}")
```

Read that last line again: the least dense thing in the Universe **is the
Universe**, about $10^{-29}\ \text{g/cm}^3$, six protons per cubic metre.

### Your turn: interrogate the densities {#sec-ex-density}

You have `rho_all` for all 29 objects. Rank everything by density and
print a table from densest to fluffiest, with the group and the density of
each object. Then answer from your output: which **group** owns the top of
the table, and how many decades of density separate a red giant from a
white dwarf, two objects of nearly the same *mass*?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_density
import js
import numpy as np
from pyodide.http import open_url
DATA_URL = js.location.href.split("site_libs/")[0] + "data/"
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
rows = [line.split(",") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]
names  = [r[0] for r in rows]
groups = [r[1] for r in rows]
mass   = np.array([float(r[2]) for r in rows])
radius = np.array([float(r[3]) for r in rows])
rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_density
# `names`, `groups`, `mass`, `radius` and `rho_all` are all loaded.
# 1. Get the object order sorted by density, densest first.
# 2. Print rank, name, group, density for every object.
# 3. Compute the red giant / white dwarf density gap in decades.

order = ______

for rank, i in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"{rank:>2}. {names[i]:<20} {groups[i]:<18} {rho_all[i]:>9.1e} g/cm³")

gap = ______
print(f"\nred giant vs white dwarf: {gap:.0f} decades of density")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_density"}
**Hint 1**: `np.argsort(rho_all)` gives indices from *smallest* to
largest; reverse it with `[::-1]` to get densest first.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_density"}
**Hint 2**: A "decade" is a factor of ten, so the gap in decades is
`np.log10(rho_wd / rho_rg)`. Get each with
`rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")]`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_density"}
**Fully worked solution:**

```python
order = np.argsort(rho_all)[::-1]

for rank, i in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"{rank:>2}. {names[i]:<20} {groups[i]:<18} {rho_all[i]:>9.1e} g/cm³")

gap = np.log10(rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")]
               / rho_all[names.index("red giant")])
print(f"\nred giant vs white dwarf: {gap:.0f} decades of density")
```

The top of the table belongs entirely to **particles**: the top quark
and Higgs boson are the densest "objects" plotted, though for them
density is a strange notion (their radius is a quantum limit, not a
surface). The red giant and white dwarf differ by roughly **12 decades**
of density despite nearly identical masses; they are the same kind of
star at two different moments of its life, which is why mass alone tells
you so little and the mass–radius *pair* tells you so much.
:::

## 4 · The two physical limits

Now the physics that gives the chart its shape. Both walls are one-line
formulas.

**The gravity wall.** Squeeze a mass $m$ into a small enough radius and
it becomes a black hole. That radius is the Schwarzschild radius
$r_s = 2Gm/c^2$; for a given radius, the heaviest possible object is
$m = rc^2/2G$: **slope +1** on our axes. Nothing can sit above this line:
an object of that mass would already have collapsed. Black holes sit
exactly *on* it; that is what a black hole is.

**The quantum wall.** Quantum mechanics denies small masses a definite
tiny size: a particle of mass $m$ cannot be localised below its Compton
wavelength $\lambda_c = \hbar / mc$, so the lightest possible object of
radius $r$ is $m = \hbar/rc$: **slope −1**. Below this line, "object"
stops meaning anything; try to confine a particle tighter and you create
new particles instead. Fundamental particles (top quark, Higgs, electron,
neutrino) are plotted *on* their Compton wavelengths; the composite proton
gets its measured charge radius.

```{pyodide}
def schwarzschild_mass(r):   # heaviest object of radius r (it's a black hole)
    return r * c**2 / (2 * G)

def compton_mass(r):         # lightest object of radius r (quantum limit)
    return hbar / (r * c)

wall_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": r_line,
    "gravity_mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
    "compton_mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
    "upper_mass_g": 1e60,
    "lower_mass_g": 1e-40,
})

gravity_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#e66852", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(),
    y=cosmos_y("gravity_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("upper_mass_g:Q"),
)

quantum_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#4269d0", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(),
    y=cosmos_y("lower_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("compton_mass_g:Q"),
)

wall_lines = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "black-hole limit"}),
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "Compton limit"}),
], ignore_index=True)

wall_line_chart = alt.Chart(wall_lines).mark_line(
    color="#171717", strokeWidth=1.5, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), detail="wall:N"
)

gravity_label = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [3e-14], "mass_g": [1e45],
    "label": ["forbidden by gravity"],
})).mark_text(
    angle=322, color="#8a3324", fontSize=14
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

quantum_label = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [3e-5], "mass_g": [1e-24],
    "label": ["quantum uncertainty"],
})).mark_text(
    angle=38, color="#1d3f8f", fontSize=14
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

(
    gravity_region
    + quantum_region
    + wall_line_chart
    + object_layers()
    + gravity_label
    + quantum_label
).properties(
    width=740,
    height=650,
    title="Nothing above the black-hole line, nothing below the Compton line",
).configure_axis(gridColor="#dddddd", gridOpacity=0.7)
```

The empty corners of Step 2 are now explained, and shaded. They are not
unexplored; they are **impossible**. This is the deepest trick in the
figure: the *absence* of data is carrying the physics, and the shading
turns absence into a statement.

One object deserves a second look. Check the top-right corner:

```{pyodide}
iU = names.index("observable Universe")
ratio = 2 * G * mass[iU] / c**2 / radius[iU]
print(f"Universe: Schwarzschild radius / actual radius = {ratio:.2f}")
```

```{pyodide}
assert 0.8 < ratio < 1.2
print("✓ the observable Universe sits ON the black-hole line")
```

The Universe's mass and radius satisfy the black-hole relation almost
exactly. Does that mean we live inside a black hole? The paper's answer
is careful: the Schwarzschild formula assumes empty space *outside* the
object, and outside our Hubble volume the density carries on much the
same, so no. But *why* the numbers land on the line so precisely is the
second exercise.

## 5 · The Planck scale, and the finished chart

Walls of slope +1 and −1 must meet. Set them equal:

$$\frac{rc^2}{2G} = \frac{\hbar}{rc}
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
r = \sqrt{\frac{2G\hbar}{c^3}},\qquad
m = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar c}{2G}}.$$

```{pyodide}
r_x = np.sqrt(2 * G * hbar / c**3)
m_x = np.sqrt(hbar * c / (2 * G))
l_p = np.sqrt(hbar * G / c**3)    # Planck length
m_p = np.sqrt(hbar * c / G)       # Planck mass

print(f"walls cross at    r = {r_x:.2e} cm,  m = {m_x:.2e} g")
print(f"Planck scale:   l_p = {l_p:.2e} cm, m_p = {m_p:.2e} g")
```

```{pyodide}
assert abs(r_x / (np.sqrt(2) * l_p) - 1) < 1e-6
assert abs(m_x / (m_p / np.sqrt(2)) - 1) < 1e-6
print("✓ the walls cross at the Planck scale (times a factor of √2)")
```

The crossing point is the **Planck scale**: about $10^{-33}$ cm and
$2\times10^{-5}$ g, the mass of a flea's egg compressed to a point
$10^{20}$ times smaller than a proton. The smallest possible object is a
Planck-mass black hole, which the paper calls an **instanton**: the only
thing that is simultaneously as small as gravity allows and as small as
quantum mechanics allows. Left of the Planck length, physics has no
tested theory at all; the paper shades it "sub-Planckian unknown", and
so will we.

Now assemble everything (regions, walls, density skeleton, objects,
apex):

```{pyodide}
subplanck_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "left": [1e-35], "right": [l_p],
    "bottom": [1e-40], "top": [1e60],
})

subplanck_region = alt.Chart(subplanck_data).mark_rect(
    color="#555555", opacity=0.25
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x("left"), x2=alt.X2("right:Q"),
    y=cosmos_y("bottom"), y2=alt.Y2("top:Q"),
)

instanton_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [l_p], "mass_g": [m_p],
    "label": ["instanton (Planck scale)"],
})

instanton_point = alt.Chart(instanton_data).mark_point(
    shape="diamond", filled=True, size=100, color="#171717"
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y())

instanton_label = alt.Chart(instanton_data).mark_text(
    align="left", dx=8, dy=12, fontSize=10, color="#171717"
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

def chart_annotation(label, x, y, angle=0, colour="#171717", size=11):
    data = pd.DataFrame({
        "radius_cm": [x], "mass_g": [y], "label": [label]
    })
    return alt.Chart(data).mark_text(
        angle=angle, color=colour, fontSize=size
    ).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

final_annotations = (
    chart_annotation("forbidden by gravity", 3e-14, 1e45,
                     angle=330, colour="#8a3324", size=14)
    + chart_annotation("quantum uncertainty", 3e-5, 1e-24,
                       angle=30, colour="#1d3f8f", size=14)
    + chart_annotation("sub-Planckian unknown", 1.7e-35, 1e10,
                       angle=270, colour="#444444")
    + chart_annotation("black holes", 1e-24, 3e6, angle=330)
    + chart_annotation("Compton limit", 2.5e-10, 3e-21, angle=30)
)

(
    gravity_region
    + quantum_region
    + subplanck_region
    + wall_line_chart
    + density_line_chart
    + object_layers()
    + instanton_point
    + instanton_label
    + final_annotations
    + density_labels
).properties(
    width=760,
    height=700,
    title="Everything in the Universe, one chart, after Lineweaver & Patel (2023)",
).configure_axis(gridColor="#dddddd", gridOpacity=0.7)
```

That is the triangle of everything: gravity above, quantum uncertainty
below, the unknown to the left, the Universe pinned to the top of the
gravity wall, and every known thing strung out on density lines in
between.

### Your turn: put the Universe on the wall {#sec-ex-hubble}

The Universe's point was given to you in the table. Derive it. All you
need is the Hubble constant. The radius of the observable Universe is the
Hubble radius $r_H = c/H_0$; its average density is the critical density
$\rho_c = 3H_0^2 / 8\pi G$; and its mass is that density times the volume
of the Hubble sphere. Then test whether your derived Universe lands on
the black-hole line.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_hubble
import numpy as np
G    = 6.674e-8       # [cm^3 g^-1 s^-2]
c    = 2.998e10       # [cm/s]
H0   = 70 / 3.086e19  # [1/s]
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_hubble
# Constants G, c and H0 are loaded (cgs units).
# 1. Hubble radius, critical density, and the mass of the Hubble sphere.
# 2. Schwarzschild radius of that mass: how does it compare to r_H?

r_H   = ______
rho_c = ______
m_U   = ______

r_s = 2 * G * m_U / c**2
print(f"r_H = {r_H:.2e} cm   m_U = {m_U:.2e} g")
print(f"Schwarzschild radius of the Universe's mass: {r_s:.2e} cm")
print(f"ratio r_s / r_H = {r_s / r_H:.3f}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_hubble"}
**Hint 1**: All three formulas are written in the task text above; your
job is to translate them into code, in order, using the constants
provided. Watch the parentheses in the critical-density formula.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_hubble"}
**Hint 2**: If your ratio comes out wildly far from 1 (say $10^{-57}$),
you almost certainly forgot to cube $r_H$ in the volume of the sphere.
:::

**How to know you got it.** No solution button; the derivation is
yours. Done right, the ratio comes out **suspiciously exact**. That
exactness is itself the final puzzle: take the three formulas you just
coded, substitute them into each other on paper, and watch what happens
to the constants. What you find is a lesson about reading charts, not
just making them: when a data point lands perfectly on a theory line,
always ask whether the two were secretly computed from the same
ingredients.

{{< include _instructor-c.qmd >}}

## What went into the chart

Count the ingredients you actually used:

- **one curated table**: 29 rows, every value an order-of-magnitude
  sketch, sources mixed from measurement (Earth), convention (the 50-cm
  spherical human), and definition (black-hole radii);
- **two log axes**: doing more work than everything else combined,
  turning 90 orders of magnitude into a readable square and power laws
  into straight lines;
- **one fact about spheres**: $m \propto \rho r^3$, which organises all
  atomic matter onto one line and all nuclear matter onto another;
- **two formulas**: $r_s = 2Gm/c^2$ and $\lambda_c = \hbar/mc$, drawn
  not as data but as *walls*, turning empty space into a claim;
- **annotation**: region labels, line labels, direct point labels: the
  difference between a scatter plot and an explanation.

That is the whole machine. The famous figure is not famous for its data
(half its rows you could have written down yourself) but for its
*framing*: pick axes everything shares, let physics draw the boundaries,
and the emptiness becomes the story.

## Sources

- Lineweaver, C. H. & Patel, V. M. (2023) *All objects and some
  questions*, American Journal of Physics 91:819–825
  ([doi:10.1119/5.0150209](https://doi.org/10.1119/5.0150209)), the
  original Figure 2, which this page rebuilds in simplified form (we omit
  the cosmological-epoch background shading and plot a smaller object
  sample).
- `objects_universe.csv` is curated for this course: masses and radii are
  order-of-magnitude values assembled from standard references; the
  human and whale entries deliberately reproduce the paper's values,
  sphericity and all. Fundamental particles are plotted at their Compton
  wavelengths (the proton at its measured charge radius); black holes at
  their Schwarzschild radii.
- Constants: CODATA values rounded to 4 significant figures;
  $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc.
